 29|
 30|## 1. OVERVIEW
 31|
 32|### Purpose
 33|
 34|Provides the flow-mode workflow for drawing a diagram on a FigJam board. Flow Mode owns the route, the type choice, the intake, the model, the check, the gate, the read-back and the reply. The write composes a framed board from the checked model through one of three routes, and the board is the only deliverable.
 35|
 36|### When to Use
 37|
 38|Use Flow Mode for any diagram on a FigJam board:
 39|- A user flow drawn from screenshots, Figma frames or a product doc
 40|- A process or decision flow, with a lane per team when work changes hands
 41|- An architecture, a sequence of calls, a state machine, a data model or a dated plan
 42|
 43|Use another mode instead for:
 44|- Figma feedback on spacing, copy or alignment, which is a Task
 45|- A written description of a flow or a system, which is a Doc
 46|- A defect seen while walking the flow, which is a Bug
 47|
 48|### Command: `$flow`
 49|
 50|- **Alias:** `$figjam`. There is no single-letter alias, so `$f` stays free
 51|- **Purpose:** Draw a diagram on a FigJam board
 52|- **Output:** The board URL, one read-back line and the HVR self-scan line, never a file
 53|- **Thinking:** Standard energy, which caps the intake at three rounds, and Deep energy is five. Quick energy is zero rounds: it fills the Brief in Section 4 from the sources and the defaults rather than asking, marks each row it inferred `assumed` with what would settle it and sends one message with the rows, the chosen type and an offer to draw unless corrected. Just-do-it wording selects Quick and never Raw, which skips the phase flow. No energy skips the check or the gate, because they guard a write to a shared Figma plan
 54|
 55|---
 56|
 57|## 2. WORKFLOW
 58|
 59|1. **Route.** `$flow`, `$figjam`, FigJam output wording or a request to add notes to or change a FigJam board selects this mode. Notes on a board already written follow `references/hybrid-workflow.md` on node ids from a `get_figjam` read, and a change to what the board says is a revision that composes the board again, as Section 6 sets out
 60|2. **Pick the type.** Name the reader's question and the type that answers it, as Section 3 sets out, and load that type's reference and template. The outline pass below tests that answer against a second framing before anything is drawn
 61|3. **Intake.** Read every source by its input type, as Section 4 sets out, classify each claim, set the detail level, the audience and the reading distance, and ask the questions the brief leaves open until the draw-ready threshold below is met, then settle the one sentence the board answers. That sentence is the `userIntent` the remove test and the write call both use. The intake writes one record per item, node or edge, before any Mermaid, into the provenance table that `assets/flow-templates.md` Section 3 lays out: the item, its kind, its source, its source class, its confidence and the rung of the inference ladder in Section 4 that reached it. Where a frame name and the heading a reader sees differ, both land in the row and the heading labels the node. No item reaches the model without a row
 62|4. **Model.** Run the outline pass below first, so the shape is agreed as text before a line is drawn. Then write one Mermaid block per diagram in the type's grammar, drawn from the provenance rows the intake wrote, so no node and no connector appears in Mermaid that has no row. A shape first seen while writing is read into a row before it is kept. A process or an architecture starts with a `%% type:` line. The board's title, subtitle, source line and zones ride on `%% title:`, `%% subtitle:`, `%% source:` and `%% zone:` comment lines, as `assets/flow-templates.md` Section 1 sets out. The model is working data, never a deliverable
 63|5. **Check.** Run `scripts/flow_check.py` on the model. A failing model is fixed or split, then checked again, and nothing is written until every diagram passes
 64|6. **Quality pass.** Walk `references/quality-rubric.md`. The script checks what a script can see, and the rubric checks whether every node earns its place
 65|7. **Gate.** State the Brief's question and the outcome the board must deliver, so the yes covers the purpose and not only the destination, then the three glance lines `references/quality-rubric.md` Section 3 asks to be written before the model, the first glance the board must win, the second glance that advances it and the last glance that may wait. The first glance is the accented node on a user flow or a process, marked by its one required `style` line, and on any other type the node, message or task an optional `%% focus:` line names. The gate then gives the target plan and file, what will be written, any planned extensions, the calls the write will spend and the rollback in one message and waits for a yes. On the composed route the calls are `whoami` for the plan, `create_new_file` for a new board, the `use_figma` call that composes each diagram and the `get_figjam` read-back. Figma limits a Starter plan and a View or Collab seat to six tool calls a month. Read tools count against that allowance and some write tools are exempt, so such a user may spend the whole allowance on one or two boards. The file is a new file, which the write creates first, or the `fileKey` of a board this work already wrote. A FigJam file has one page and no write can add another, so a page is never the target. An earlier yes never carries over to a new board. The gate is its own reply, sent only after the playback's answer, as Section 8 sets out under The gate is its own reply
 66|8. **Write.** Compose the board with `scripts/compose_board.py` and one `use_figma` call per diagram. Fall back to `generate_diagram` only when `use_figma` is not connected, and to the `fj` route when neither hosted tool is connected and the type allows it, as Section 6 sets out
 67|9. **Extend.** Only when the gate named an extension, add it through `references/hybrid-workflow.md`
 68|10. **Read back.** Read the written board with `get_figjam` on the board id the write returned, never from memory, and compare it with the model as Section 7 and the type's reference set out. The composing call returns a screenshot of the whole board, which is the overview, and `get_figjam` returns the outline with a screenshot of each node. A node that needs its own view is read with `get_screenshot` and the node id from that read, because the tool fails without one. Then check the overview for stretching, a label cut off, overlap, a connector crossing, an edge that reads as joining the wrong node, a colour that does not match its entry in the key and whether the board answers the `userIntent` sentence. A finding there goes on a `Finding:` line of the reply, and it is fixed only by reshaping the model and recomposing after a yes, inside the two-attempt bound Section 9 sets. Section 7 names the read for each route. The rows that fail silently are read back the same way, one at a time and before the gate. Each provenance row whose class is not current behavior or whose edge is inferred gets one re-read of its source, and that row records the reason. A row that quotes a source line is not re-read
 69|11. **Reply.** Deliver as Section 8 sets out

 71|### The draw-ready threshold and the stop rule
 72|
 73|Two failures bracket the intake. Drawing before the rows are covered puts a guessed feature on the board, and asking past a settled row spends a round the reader did not need. The brief that Section 4 sets out is the count, so the threshold and the stop rule can both be read off it.
 74|
 75|Flow Mode draws when all three hold:
 76|- No row of the brief is unasked
 77|- The reader and the question are settled
 78|- At most two rows are assumed, and each one names how it gets settled
 79|
 80|Stop asking at the first of these that is true:
 81|- The brief is complete and the user confirms it
 82|- Two rounds in a row change no row
 83|- The user says stop
 84|- The energy cap is reached
 85|
 86|The cap counts rounds, never questions, because one round is one message however many questions it carries. A later round asks only about a row the sources and the last answers left unasked, such as a gap the answers opened, and never repeats a question. Quick energy is zero rounds, Standard is three and Deep is five. At the cap Flow Mode draws with the assumed rows named, or where the sources cannot carry a diagram it says so and offers a table, as Section 3 sets out. A row still unasked at the cap is named as assumed, never left silent.
 87|
 88|### The outline pass
 89|
 90|Agree what the board says before any layout is judged. A layout reviewed before the message is agreed is a review of the wrong thing.
 91|
 92|The pass offers three proposals, cheapest first, and none of them is a stop of its own. The outline, the two framings and the look ride in the playback, and the sketch is the checked model the gate shows, so the run still stops only at an intake round, the playback and the gate. Each proposal states what the sources already show and a recommended answer with a one-line reason, so a user who does not know can accept it, and the one answer to the playback settles them all.
 93|
 94|- **The outline.** One line per node and one per edge, in drawing order, each naming its row in the Brief. The first line is the `userIntent` sentence, the reader's question in one sentence, and that same sentence is passed to the write call. The remove test runs here, on text, where a cut costs no read call
 95|- **Two named framings.** Say what each framing buys and what it costs, such as a happy path with the branches beside it against a state map that shows every exit. Name the one you recommend and why
 96|- **The sketch.** The checked Mermaid model the gate shows in chat, never written to a board before the gate's yes, so the shape can be argued with before it costs a write
 97|
 98|The look is settled last, in five proposed choices:
 99|- The node the colour marks, by the keep-one test in `quality-rubric.md` Section 3: which end is the goal, whether an end is a failure and whether one step is in focus
100|- The detail level and the audience, read from the rows the intake captured rather than asked again
101|- Whether the board needs zones, and where each one starts, since a `%% zone:` line is a choice, not a default
102|- The title, the one-sentence subtitle under it and the source line under the key
103|- Four critique questions the gate answers about the sketch, opening with where the eye goes first and whether that is the node the board most needs read
104|
105|An unanswered proposal never stops the run. The recommended answer stands and is marked assumed. The playback names it, so the user can correct it before anything is written.

109|## 3. PICK THE DIAGRAM TYPE
110|
111|The question the reader needs answered picks the type. Ask before drawing when two types fit, such as an architecture and a sequence for the same system, because they answer different questions.
112|
113|The Brief's first round, the reader, the question and the outcome, runs before the type is chosen, because the reader's question picks the type. The type is then challenged, and the later rounds ask what that type needs, because types do not want the same sources: a state diagram's actors are not a sequence's participants, so rows asked ahead of the type answer questions another diagram owns.
114|
115|| The reader asks | Type | Reference |
116||---|---|---|
117|| Which screens does a person pass through, and where do they choose? | User flow | `references/types/user-flow.md` |
118|| Who does what, in which order, and where does work change hands? | Process | `references/types/process.md` |
119|| What parts make up this system and how do they connect? | Architecture | `references/types/architecture.md` |
120|| In what order do these parties exchange messages? | Sequence | `references/types/sequence.md` |
121|| Which states exist and what moves the thing between them? | State | `references/types/state.md` |
122|| Which entities exist, what fields do they carry and how do they relate? | ER | `references/types/er.md` |
123|| Which tasks and phases are active when? | Gantt | `references/types/gantt.md` |
124|
125|### A type the user names
126|
127|A named type is compared with what the brief describes before the intake asks anything else. A mismatch, such as a state diagram asked for over a path through screens, is asked about once, naming the type asked for, what the brief describes and the recommended type. A requested type changes only on an answer to a question that named the change, so a bare yes to another question never swaps it.
128|
129|### Testing the type against what it needs
130|
131|The pick is a claim about the input. The needs table in Section 4 says what that claim rests on, so read the input against the table's row for the chosen type before the intake asks anything else. A type whose needs the input cannot meet draws a diagram of an imagined system. A state diagram for a billing screen whose screenshots show no events has no events to draw.
132|
133|A need the input does not meet takes one of three routes, and the cheapest that works is the one taken:
134|- **One question.** The input almost carries the need, such as a filename that names the trigger but not the screen it opens. The gap is asked once, with the AI's reading and a recommended answer
135|- **A different type.** The input carries another type's needs better. The reader's question is read again, because a question about states is sometimes answered by the screens that set them, and the swap is offered with its reason
136|- **A named gap.** No question settles the need and no other type fits, so the need stays unmet and is named as a gap in the playback before the gate
137|
138|The route taken is recorded against the need it settled. A later reader can then see why the board holds this type. A need left unmet reaches the reply's `Left out:` line as a named omission.
139|
140|### Before drawing at all
141|
142|Would the reader learn more from a diagram than from a list, a table or a paragraph? Two or three steps in a row are a list. When the answer is no, say so and offer the list.
143|
144|### The challenge ladder
145|
146|Five rungs in cost order, so the cheapest question comes before any source is read. Rung two can end the work with an offer, and rung five makes every cut above it visible to the user.
147|
148|1. **What must this board not do.** Ask it in the request's own words before any source is read, with the AI's reading of the request and a recommended answer, and ask it even when the request names no type. A board that refused nothing is the expensive case
149|2. **Would a list, a table or a paragraph serve better.** The test above answers it, and a yes ends the work with that offer
150|3. **The remove test on the outline.** Cut every step, node and connector the reader would not miss before a single line of Mermaid is written, as `references/quality-rubric.md` Section 2 sets out
151|4. **Split rather than shrink.** A model over budget becomes an overview board and a detail board, offered together, never a thinner board that drops a step
152|5. **Name every omission.** Every cut, every split and every point the sources left open is named in the reply's `Left out:` line, so the user sees what the board does not hold
153|
154|### What Flow Mode does not draw
155|
156|The composer draws the seven types in the table above and no other. Neither it nor Figma's `generate_diagram` fallback draws a pie chart, a mindmap, a Venn diagram, a class diagram, a journey, a timeline, a quadrant chart, a C4 diagram, a git graph or a requirement diagram. Say so plainly rather than drawing a stand-in. Offer the nearest type Flow Mode does draw when one answers the same question:
157|
158|| Asked for | Nearest drawable type |
159||---|---|
160|| Journey | A user flow of the screens it visits |
161|| Timeline | A gantt chart, with each event as a milestone |
162|| Class diagram | An ER diagram of the data the classes hold |
163|| C4 container or context | An architecture |
164|| Pie, mindmap, Venn, quadrant | None. Offer a table or a list in a Doc |

168|## 4. INTAKE
169|
170|Ask the intake as an interview, in the three rounds `assets/flow-templates.md` Section 5 sets out, so an answer in one round settles what the next may ask. Every question there carries the AI's reading of the input, a recommended answer and the one line of reason for it, so an unanswered question never blocks the work.
171|
172|### The Brief
173|
174|Nine rows hold what the intake learned, and the rows are filled as each source is read by the input types below. Each row carries a value, the source it came from and one status:
175|
176|| Row | Holds |
177||---|---|
178|| Reader | Who the board is for and the question they bring to it |
179|| Question | The question the diagram answers, in one sentence |
180|| Outcome | What the reader can decide or do after reading the board |
181|| Scope | What the board covers and what it leaves out |
182|| Entry | Where the flow starts |
183|| Exit | Where it ends and what counts as done |
184|| Actors | Who or what moves the work along |
185|| Decisions and states | The choices a person makes and the states the thing passes through |
186|| Sources and class | Each source read, with its class |
187|
188|A row carries one of four statuses:
189|
190|- `captured` when a supplied source states it
191|- `corrected` when the user changed what a source said

396|Each type's reference names what its read-back counts. Every read-back compares the board with the model, never with memory:
397|
398|- Every node, state, participant, entity or task, by count and by label
399|- Every connector, message, transition or relationship, joining the same two ends in the same direction with the same label
400|- What the type adds, such as labelled decision exits, lanes, attributes or milestones
401|
402|Direction comes from the connector, never from its position on the board. The two endpoint ids say which node each end attaches to. The two end caps say which way the arrow points. An arrow at the end is forward, an arrow at the start is reversed, an arrow at both ends is two-way and no arrow is undirected. A connector that reads reversed or two-way where the model drew one direction is a mismatch. So is a connector whose two ends are swapped. An ER connector is the exception, because a relationship has no direction. The composer draws it with no arrow at either end and writes its cardinality into the label, such as `holds (1 to 0..n)`, with a solid line for an identifying relationship and a dashed one otherwise, so it is compared on its two ends, its label and its line. On the generated route no live read has yet shown the generator drawing cardinality markers, so an ER connector whose caps read plain there is counted on its two ends and its label alone.
403|
404|A connector with a missing end, or an end pinned to the page or the canvas rather than to a node, is a mismatch named as dangling. It is never matched by its position.
405|
406|On the composed route the read is `get_figjam` on the board id the write returned. It reports each section by name, each shape with its label text and each connector with its layer name and its two endpoint ids, so the board is matched to the model by name and by id:
407|
408|- A node is a shape whose id the write returned in its node list, carrying the label the model gives it. Shapes inside the `Key` section are samples, and the empty 16 pixel ellipses are anchors that hold a routed connector, so neither counts as a node
409|- A connector is a connector named `edge:<from>-><to>`, one per model edge. A routed edge reaches its target through anchors, so its start is an anchor rather than the source: follow the connectors named `leg:<from>-><to>:<n>`, from the highest `<n>` down to `:1`, back through their anchors to the source node. The label sits on the leg that carries it
410|- A sequence message is named `edge:<from>-><to>:<n>`, with its order as the last part. Its ends hold anchors on the two lifelines rather than the participant boxes, so the name carries both parties and the screenshot shows the line between them
411|- A zone is a section named after its label, and its nodes sit inside it
412|
413|On the generated route the read is `get_figjam`, node by node, matching shapes by their label because the generator writes no layer names. On the `fj` route it is `fj nodes -l`. When only a screenshot could be read, the read was visual, because a picture cannot prove which nodes a connector joins.
414|
415|A board that already holds content can be slower to read than a fresh one. A read that times out is retried on fewer nodes at a time, halving the count until the read returns. A timeout is never proof that a node or a connector is missing. When the file held content before the write, the read-back reads those nodes again and compares their count, position and size with the read taken before the write, so the reply can say the content already there was left as it was.
416|
417|---
418|
419|## 8. DELIVERY
420|
421|The reply carries the board, its proof and the self-scan, and nothing else. Anything the user must know or answer has a place above the self-scan.
422|
423|- The first line is the board URL
424|- The second line is the read-back, counts measured on the board against the model, in the words the type's reference uses: `Read-back: 8 of 8 nodes, 8 of 8 connectors, 2 of 2 decision exits labelled`. When the connected tools include no read tool, the line is `Read-back: not possible, the connector has no read tool`, and the board is never called done. When the board URL landed in a re-saved artifact, the line ends with the name of the file the artifact was saved to. On a matched read-back the same line also names the first glance in one clause, such as `, first glance: the failed payment`, so the user knows what should win before the board is opened
425|- When the write added extensions, the next line counts them: `Extensions: 4 of 4 pins, 4 of 4 legend stickies, 0 overlaps`, or `Extensions: 2 of 2 notes, 0 overlaps` for single stickies
426|- When the provenance table lists items left out, the next line names them as `Left out: <item>, <reason>`, so the user sees what the board does not hold. On a split or a cut, the reason names the detail level and the cut, such as `Left out: the retry path, split into a second diagram`
427|- A contradicted item appears in that same line with both of its sources and the reason it was not drawn, so a finding the sources disagree on is still visible to the reader
428|- When the file holds two or more diagrams, the read-back line also names the board a reader opens first, by the ordinal and the name in its title, in one clause such as `, start here: 1. Signup`
429|- A finding from the read-back, a warning the write returned, a `DESIGN` line the composer printed, an open item or a question the user must answer is one `Finding:` line each, placed above the self-scan. A `DESIGN` finding names the token, what the design file asked for and the value the board drew instead. Where the board landed, the tools used, the cleanup and the rollback are not part of the reply
430|- The last line is the HVR self-scan in the shape `AGENTS.md` step 8 sets, counted on the labels written to the board. Nothing follows it, not a note, a finding or a question. Flow Mode is exempt from the export steps, never from the scan
431|- A read-back that does not match is reported as measured, with the missing or extra items named. The board is never called done on a mismatch
432|- A paired request, a route carrying `then: "FLOW"`, delivers the artifact first under its own mode's protocol: written, exported and read back. That reply ends on Flow Mode's playback, which waits for its own answer, with no ClickUp offer. Flow Mode then runs with that artifact as its product-doc source, under its own pre-write check and its own yes at the write gate
433|- When the request came with an artifact and the read-back matched the model, a Task, Bug, Story or Epic uses its `Flows` group and a Doc uses `Related references`, with the diagram’s name as the link text. The paired-output route and link placement are owned here
434|- The artifact is then saved again at its existing export path and read back, so the file the user keeps carries the link. That save is the artifact's own export step, not a Flow Mode one
435|- When only a screenshot could be read, the read-back line ends with `, read visually`
436|- No file is written to `export/`, and no Mermaid, HTML, SVG or PNG file is left behind. The check reads the model from a temporary file outside the repository, deleted once the reply is sent

438|### The playback
439|
440|Each round of intake opens with a short replay of the rows settled so far, one row per line, each in the words the product uses. The replay sits above the round's next question, so a wrong row is corrected before more answers build on it.
441|
442|Before the model there is one full playback, and it waits for one answer. It states the Brief's question and its outcome, what each source settled, every row still open and every fact it assumed. That answer is not the gate's yes, because the gate asks about a write and the playback asks about the reading.
443|
444|An unanswered question never stops the work. The reading proceeds on the recommendation the question gave, the fact is marked assumed and the playback names it, so the user corrects it before anything is written. A yes moves the work on to the model. A correction changes that row and the playback runs again over the rows it touched.
445|
446|The playback is not one of the five reply lines. It runs before the write, and the reply states only the board, the read-back, the extensions, what was left out and the self-scan.
447|
448|### The gate is its own reply
449|
450|The playback and the gate are two replies, never one. The playback comes before the model, so its reply carries no Mermaid, no check result and no composed code. It ends on its one question about the reading, names no plan, lists no calls and never asks whether to write. The gate reply follows the playback's answer, and its one question asks about the write alone. No question is ever worded so that one yes covers both, such as a yes that confirms the reading and the write together.
451|
452|Only a yes to the gate's own question writes. A yes to the playback, an answer to an intake round, a request to use the recommended answers or a yes to a question no reply asked never writes. Before the playback has had its answer, the reply to any of those is the playback.   1|# Roamstay company context
  2|
  3|Maintained by Leila, Product Operations Lead. Last reviewed on 2026-09-18.
  4|
  5|Roamstay is a hotel booking marketplace. Guests search and book stays at hotels, guesthouses and serviced apartments, and partners list and run their properties on it. About 18,000 properties are live, across Europe and the United States.
  6|
  7|## Product and surfaces
  8|
  9|Roamstay has three surfaces. Each has its own owners and its own release rhythm.
 10|
 11|| Surface | Used by | Platforms | Covers |
 12||---------|---------|-----------|--------|
 13|| Guest app | Guests | iOS, Android, web | Search, property page, checkout, trips, account, chat with Guest Support |
 14|| Partner Hub | Partners | Web, built for desktop | Property profile, rooms, rates and availability, policies, city tax, payouts, bookings list, guest reviews |
 15|| Back office | Ops agents, Guest Support | Web, staff only | Booking lookup, refunds and rebooking, partner verification, go-live review, payout holds |
 16|
 17|When a ticket says Guest app without a platform, it means iOS, Android and web together. The web version uses the same services as the apps, but it is built and released on its own.
 18|
 19|Partner Hub is where a partner changes what guests see. A price, a photo, a cancellation policy or a city tax rule saved there reaches the Guest app through `partner-service` within 5 minutes.
 20|
 21|Back office is invisible to guests and partners. Every refund, rebooking or payout hold made there is logged against the agent who made it.
 22|
 23|## Personas and roles
 24|
 25|| Persona | Works in | What they do |
 26||---------|----------|--------------|
 27|| Guest | Guest app | Searches, books and manages stays. Can book signed in or with an email address only |
 28|| Partner | Partner Hub | Runs one or more properties. Partner Hub users are Owner, Manager or Front desk, and only an Owner can change payout details |
 29|| Ops agent | Back office | Roamstay staff who verify new partners, set up and check properties before go-live and handle partner escalations |
 30|| Guest Support agent | Back office and the support desk tool | Answers guest chats and emails in six languages and escalates product defects to the owning squad as a ticket |
 31|
 32|Guest Support is its own team inside Operations, next to the Ops agents. A defect reaches a squad as a Guest Support ticket with a priority of Low, Medium, High or Urgent, set by the Tier 2 agent who escalates it.
 33|
 34|## Glossary
 35|
 36|| Term | Meaning |
 37||------|---------|
 38|| Stay | One booking's dates at one property, counted in nights. Check-in on a Monday and check-out on a Thursday is 3 nights |
 39|| Property | A hotel, guesthouse or apartment building listed by a partner, identified by a numeric property ID |
 40|| Room type | A kind of room at a property, such as Double room or Family suite, with a maximum occupancy |
 41|| Rate plan | A price for a room type with its own cancellation policy and payment option. One room type often has two or three |
 42|| Free cancellation | A rate plan policy that refunds the guest in full if they cancel before a deadline the partner sets |
 43|| Non-refundable | A rate plan policy with no refund after booking, usually priced lower |
 44|| City tax | A local tax the partner enters in Partner Hub, per adult per night or per stay. It shows as its own `City tax` line in the price breakdown and is part of the total |
 45|| Pay now | The guest pays the full total at booking, and the payment provider charges the card |
 46|| Pay at property | The guest's card is stored as a guarantee and the guest pays the property on arrival |
 47|| Booking reference | `RS-` followed by six letters and digits. It is on the confirmation screen, in every email and in Back office |
 48|| `payment_pending` | The booking state between Pay now and the payment provider's confirmation |
 49|| Go-live | The moment a new property becomes bookable in the Guest app |
 50|| Payout | Money Roamstay sends a partner for completed stays, after commission |
 51|
 52|## Services and integrations
 53|
 54|| Service | Owner squad | Responsibility |
 55||---------|-------------|----------------|
 56|| `search-service` | Search | Availability search, ranking, filters and paging, at `25 results` per page |
 57|| `booking-service` | Booking | Creates bookings, owns booking states and references, sends confirmation emails |
 58|| `payments-service` | Payments | Card payments, refunds and payouts with the payment provider, and the webhooks it sends back |
 59|| `partner-service` | Partner | Properties, room types, rate plans, policies, city tax rules and partner users |
 60|| `events-collector` | Data | Receives analytics events from the apps, the web and the services |
 61|
 62|Third parties appear by role in tickets and docs, never by name:
 63|
 64|- The payment provider takes card payments for Pay now, stores cards for Pay at property and sends partner payouts. Only `payments-service` talks to it, and it reports payment results back by webhook
 65|- The map provider serves map tiles and geocoding for search and the property page
 66|- The email delivery provider sends booking confirmations for `booking-service` and partner emails for `partner-service`
 67|- A channel manager is a partner's own tool for pushing rates and availability to several booking sites at once. It connects to `partner-service` through the partner API
 68|- The identity verification provider checks the identity documents of property owners during partner verification

 71|
 72|Product and engineering work in six squads: Search, Booking, Payments, Partner, Ops Tools and Data. A Design System group works across all of them. Each squad has a product manager, a product designer and engineers for the surfaces it owns.

 76|| `FE` | Front end | Guest app screens on iOS, Android and web, Partner Hub screens |
 77|| `BE` | Back end | Services, APIs, scheduled jobs and webhooks |

 79|| `FS` | Full stack | One change across a screen and its service, when splitting it would ship half a feature |

Two titles from the current backlog: `FE - Partner Hub - PHUB - Bulk rate editor` and `BO - Back office - OPS - Refund reason codes`.

 88|
 89|| Code | Area | Owner squad |
 90||------|------|-------------|
 91|| `SRCH` | Search form, date picker, results list, filters, sort, map | Search |

101|
102|## Platforms and app versions
103|
104|| Platform | Current version | Released | Minimum OS |
105||----------|-----------------|----------|------------|
106|| iOS | `8.12.0` | `2026-09-16` | iOS 16 |
107|| Android | `8.12.1` | `2026-09-16` | Android 9 |
108|| Web | Continuous deploys | Several times a day | Last two major versions of the main browsers |
109|
110|The apps ship on a two-week release train. The branch is cut on a Monday and the builds go to the stores on the Wednesday after. The previous train was 8.11.2 on both platforms, released on 2026-09-02.
111|
112|Android went out as 8.12.1 because the 8.12.0 build was turned back by the store over a permissions text, so the two apps carry different numbers for the same train. Android rolls out in stages over 5 days, iOS to everyone on release day.
113|
114|Apps below 8.6.0 show a forced update screen. Partner Hub and Back office are web only and deploy continuously, like the web version of the Guest app.
115|
116|## Currencies and locales
117|
118|Roamstay supports five currencies: `EUR`, `GBP`, `USD`, `CHF` and `SEK`. A partner sets one currency per property in Partner Hub, and the Guest app shows and charges prices in that currency. There is no currency conversion.
119|
120|Services and events carry money as an integer in minor units. The apps format it for the guest's locale, so the same amount shows as €1,240.50 in `en-GB` and as 1.240,50 € in `de-DE`.
121|
122|| Locale | Language | Notes |
123||--------|----------|-------|
124|| `en-GB` | English | Default, and the fallback for any missing string |
125|| `en-US` | English | US spelling, week starts on Sunday |
126|| `de-DE` | German | Strings run about 30% longer than English, check button widths |
127|| `fr-FR` | French | Space before the currency sign in prices |
128|| `es-ES` | Spanish | Space before the currency sign in prices |
129|| `it-IT` | Italian | Space before the currency sign in prices |
130|| `nl-NL` | Dutch | Currency sign before the amount, with a space |
131|
132|Every locale except `en-US` starts the week on Monday. The apps follow the device locale for dates and prices, and the web follows the browser locale. Partner Hub is available in the same seven locales.
133|
134|## Key flows
135|
136|### Search
137|
138|The guest enters a destination, check-in and check-out dates, guests and rooms. A stay runs from 1 night to `30 nights` and check-in can be at most `365 days` ahead. One search covers up to `8 rooms`. `search-service` returns `25 results` per page, sorted by Recommended. The apps load the next page on scroll. The filter sheet holds two filters today, Price and Star rating.
139|
140|### Property page
141|
142|The property page shows photos, room types and, for each room type, its rate plans with their cancellation policy and payment option. A partner can set a minimum stay for the property, which the date picker applies on this page.
143|
144|### Checkout and payment
145|
146|The guest enters their details and picks a rate plan's payment option. The price breakdown lists the room price per night and the total, with a `City tax` line between them when the property charges it.
147|
148|With `Pay now`, the payment provider charges the full total, city tax included. The booking waits in `payment_pending` until the payment provider confirms by webhook, then moves to confirmed. A booking still in `payment_pending` after `30 minutes` expires and its room goes back on sale.
149|
150|With `Pay at property`, the card is stored as a guarantee and the booking confirms at once. The guest pays the property on arrival, city tax included.
151|
152|### Confirmation and trips
153|
154|The confirmation screen shows the booking reference, dates, guests and the total. `booking-service` sends the confirmation email at the same moment. The stay then lives under Trips, where the guest can view it, change dates or cancel.
155|
156|### Cancellation
157|
158|Before the free cancellation deadline, the guest cancels under Trips and the refund goes back to the card through the payment provider. After the deadline, or on a non-refundable rate plan, the guest contacts Guest Support.
159|
160|### Partner onboarding today
161|
162|A partner signs up with a short form on the web. An Ops agent then sets up the property in Back office from the details the partner sends by email. The same agent checks identity and payout details and makes the property live.
163|
164|## Known constraints
165|
166|- A stay is at most `30 nights`, and check-in is at most `365 days` ahead
167|- One booking holds at most `8 rooms`
168|- A booking in `payment_pending` expires after `30 minutes`
169|- Prices show and charge in the property's currency, with no conversion
170|- Roamstay has no loyalty or points scheme. Guests earn no points, and there are no member tiers or member-only prices
171|- Guests who book with an email address only cannot save a card
172|- Partner Hub has no mobile app, and its screens are designed for desktop widths
173|- Back office needs a staff account and is never exposed to partners
174|- Guest Support covers 07:00 to 23:00 CET, seven days a week
175|
176|## Analytics conventions
177|
178|- Event names follow `object_action` in snake_case, with the action in the past tense
179|- A search filter the guest turns on fires `filter_applied`, with `filter_name` saying which filter
180|- Every client event carries `app_version`, `session_id`, `platform` and `locale`
181|- Server events carry the `session_id` of the request that caused them, so client and server events join on it
182|- Every event carries `source`, which is `client` or `server`
183|- Money travels as an integer in minor units, in a property whose name ends in `_minor`, with a `currency` property beside it. €129.50 is sent as `12950`
184|- Events go to `events-collector`, which accepts events from the apps, the web and the services
185|- The Data team owns the tracking plan. Each event has a row with its trigger, its properties and a status, and a squad builds an event from its row

 12|---
 13|
 14|# FigJam Type - ER
 15|
 16|An ER diagram shows which entities exist, the fields that matter on each and how they relate. The composer draws each entity as a card in the `neutral` role, its name in bold above one line per field with its keys first, and each relationship as a line with no arrow and its cardinality in the label.
 17|
 18|**Loading Condition:** CONDITIONAL, when the Flow route draws an ER diagram
 19|**Purpose:** The grammar, rules, budget and read-back for an ER diagram
 20|**Pairs With:** `assets/templates/er.md`
 21|
 22|---
 23|
 24|## 1. WHEN TO USE
 25|
 26|**The reader's question:** which entities exist, what fields do they carry and how do they relate?
 27|
 28|- A data model a story or a doc depends on, such as bookings and rooms
 29|- The tables behind a feature, read from a schema or a migration
 30|- A domain model agreed before the build, drawn from a product doc
 31|
 32|Use an architecture for services and stores, and a state diagram for one entity's lifecycle.
 33|
 34|---
 35|
 36|## 2. WHAT THE BOARD DRAWS
 37|
 38|```text
 39|erDiagram
 40|    Guest ||--o{ Booking : makes
 41|    Guest {
 42|        string id PK
 43|        string email UK
 44|    }
 45|```
 46|
 47|- A relationship is `A <cardinality> B : label`, read from A's side
 48|- `--` draws a solid line, for a child that cannot exist without its parent, and `..` a dotted one, for a looser link
 49|- An attribute is `type name`, then any of `PK`, `FK` and `UK` joined by commas, then an optional quoted comment
 50|- An alias names an entity for the board: `Property["Listed Property"] { ... }`
 51|
 52|| Cardinality | Means |
 53||---|---|
 54|| `\|\|--\|\|` | Exactly one to exactly one |
 55|| `\|\|--o\|` | Exactly one to zero or one |
 56|| `\|\|--o{` | Exactly one to zero or more |
 57|| `\|\|--\|{` | Exactly one to one or more |
 58|| `}o--o{` | Zero or more to zero or more |
 59|| `}\|--\|{` | One or more to one or more |
 60|
 61|The same ends work with `..` in place of `--`.
 62|
 63|On the board the label reads the verb and then the two ends in words, such as `makes (1 to 0..n)`. An identifying relationship is a solid line and a non-identifying one dashed, and the key names both. A `%% zone: <label>: <entity>, <entity>` line draws a tinted section around the entities of one domain.
 64|
 65|---
 66|
 67|## 3. RULES
 68|
 69|The check enforces:
 70|
 71|- **Documented cardinalities only,** each end one of `||`, `|o`, `}o` or `}|` on the left and `||`, `o|`, `o{` or `|{` on the right
 72|- **No alias inside a relationship line,** which fails to parse. Declare the alias on the entity and use the plain id in relationships
 73|- **Every relationship labelled,** a label of two or more words in double quotes, at most 40 characters
 74|- **Attributes in the documented form,** at most 10 per entity, and an entity with attributes marks its `PK`
 75|- **One spelling per type,** never `string` beside `String`
 76|- **No styling,** which neither route draws. Group a domain with a `%% zone:` line instead
 77|- **Every entity in a relationship** once there is more than one, and entity ids camelCase or PascalCase. Figma's own examples write `LINE_ITEM`, but its universal rules say an underscore can break routing, so write `LineItem` with an alias when the board should read `Line Item`
 78|- **At most 9 entities and 12 relationships,** sk-design-diagram's general budget
 79|- The shared rules: no emoji, markup or literal `\n`
 80|
 81|Judged by hand:
 82|
 83|- **Relationships first, attributes second.** The right cardinality matters more than a full column list
 84|- **Keep the 5 to 10 columns a reader needs.** The full schema belongs in the migration
 85|- **Solid for a required parent, dotted for a loose link,** chosen on purpose
 86|- **Labels are verbs from the left entity's side,** such as `makes` or `"is booked in"`
 87|- **Mark `FK` on every foreign key,** because "which field joins these?" is the question readers ask most
 88|
 89|---
 90|
 91|## 4. BUDGET AND SPLITTING
 92|
 93|Split by bounded context, such as guests and bookings in one diagram and properties and rates in another, each in the same file. When two diagrams share an entity, draw it in both and say so in the reply. At `Meeting screen` distance labels drop to 32 characters. At `Wall` distance the budget drops to 6 entities and 8 relationships, with labels at 25 characters, as the reading distance dial in `references/flow-mode.md` Section 4 sets out.
 94|
 95|---
 96|
 97|## 5. COLOUR, ZONES AND NOTES
 98|
 99|Colour by domain is what Figma ranks highest for ER, and the model now carries it: a `%% zone:` line names a domain and lists its entities, and the composer tints a section around them. An entity sits in one zone at most, and an entity in no zone sits outside every section. Sections never overlap: when the entities of two zones would interleave, the composer stacks the sections one above the other, and a board that still has zones on top of each other is refused before anything is drawn. Annotations on a column, such as a soft-delete field, go on through the pins and legend recipe in `references/hybrid-workflow.md`. A `%% focus: <id>` line may name the one node the first glance lands on. It is a comment, so the model stays styleless.
100|
101|---
102|
103|## 6. WRITING THE BOARD
104|
105|`scripts/compose_board.py` composes the model and one `use_figma` call draws the board, as `references/flow-mode.md` Section 6 sets out. On the generated fallback, `generate_diagram` takes `name`, `mermaidSyntax` and `userIntent`, and no `useArchitectureLayoutCode`. The generator strips the zone lines. The `fj` route cannot draw an ER diagram.
106|
107|---
108|
109|## 7. READ-BACK
110|

 13|
 14|# Product Owner Flow Templates
 15|
 16|Copy/apply patterns for Product Owner Flow Mode models.
 17|
 18|**Loading Condition:** CONDITIONAL, with `references/flow-mode.md` whenever Flow intent is selected
 19|**Purpose:** Provides the user-flow patterns, the provenance table every diagram type keeps and the reply shape every type delivers
 20|**Scope:** Five user-flow patterns, the intake questions, the provenance table and the reply shape. The other types keep their patterns in `assets/templates/`
 21|**Output Path:** None. The model is working data and the board is the deliverable
 22|
 23|---
 24|
 25|## 1. OVERVIEW
 26|
 27|### Purpose
 28|
 29|Every pattern below passes `scripts/flow_check.py` as a user flow, and `scripts/compose_board.py` composes it into a board. Start from the pattern closest to the flow, rename the nodes after the real screens and triggers, add the board lines below and run the check before the write gate. A process, an architecture, a sequence, a state diagram, an ER diagram or a gantt chart starts from its own file in `assets/templates/`, and keeps the provenance table and the reply shape below.
 30|
 31|### Usage
 32|
 33|- Node ids are short, stable and camelCase, because the provenance table names them, the composer names every layer after them and the generated fallback mis-routes an underscore
 34|- A label names the screen or the action a person takes, in the words the product uses, in one to four words where those words allow
 35|- A label with a parenthesis, a colon or a slash goes in double quotes, such as `pick["Pick a plan (monthly)"]`
 36|- A decision label is a question, and each exit label is one of its answers
 37|- Every connector is a solid arrow `-->`
 38|- A user flow and a process each carry exactly one `style` line, which marks the first glance. A styled goal, failing end or decision keeps its kind and takes a pink outline, and a styled step is drawn light pink. `style done fill:#CDF4D3,stroke:#66D575` makes that end the goal and the light red pair makes an end a failure. Every pair comes from `references/style-guide.md`, and any other colour is refused or counts as a second accent
 39|- Write `flowchart LR` unless the chain is short, because a board reads wider than it reads tall
 40|
 41|### Board lines
 42|
 43|The board's own text rides on `%%` comment lines, which the check ignores and the composer reads. Each one is optional, and the generated fallback strips them all:
 44|
 45|```text
 46|%% title: Start a return
 47|%% subtitle: How a customer starts a return in the app, from the order list to a confirmed return
 48|%% source: Sources: five app screenshots and the returns doc. Left out: free pickup over 100 euros, a proposal.
 49|%% zone: Find the order: orders, detail
 50|%% zone: Request the return: window, reason, method
 51|```
 52|
 53|- `%% title:` names the board. With none, the composer takes a Mermaid frontmatter title, a sequence or gantt `title` line, then `Diagram <n>`
 54|- `%% subtitle:` is one sentence under the title on who reads the board and why
 55|- `%% source:` is the line under the key naming the sources and what was left out
 56|- `%% zone: <label>: <id>, <id>` groups nodes in a tinted section. A user flow or a process without lanes reads its zones in flow order, and once a flow has zones every node sits in exactly one. An ER diagram draws each zone around its entities. Lanes and composite states are zones already, so a laned process, an architecture or a state diagram takes no zone line
 57|
 58|---
 59|
 60|## 2. PATTERNS
 61|
 62|### Linear flow
 63|
 64|```mermaid
 65|flowchart TD
 66|    start([Open the page]) --> step1[Fill in the form]
 67|    step1 --> step2[Submit]
 68|    step2 --> done([Confirmation shown])
 69|    style done fill:#CDF4D3,stroke:#66D575
 70|```
 71|
 72|### One decision
 73|
 74|```mermaid
 75|flowchart TD
 76|    start([Open the page]) --> step1[Submit the form]
 77|    step1 --> valid{Valid?}
 78|    valid -->|Yes| done([Confirmation shown])
 79|    valid -->|No| fix[Show the field errors]
 80|    fix --> step1
 81|    style done fill:#CDF4D3,stroke:#66D575
 82|```
 83|
 84|### Platform split with a merge dot
 85|
 86|```mermaid
 87|flowchart TD
 88|    start([Open the page]) --> open[Open the selector]
 89|    open --> device{Which device?}
 90|    device -->|Desktop| menu[Dropdown menu]
 91|    device -->|Mobile| sheet[Bottom sheet]
 92|    menu --> merge((.))
 93|    sheet --> merge
 94|    merge --> pick[Pick an item]
 95|    pick --> done([Item shown])
 96|    style done fill:#CDF4D3,stroke:#66D575
 97|```
 98|
 99|### Three outcomes
100|
101|```mermaid
102|flowchart TD
103|    start([Request sent]) --> result{Response?}
104|    result -->|Approved| done([Access granted])
105|    result -->|Rejected| reject([Reason shown])
106|    result -->|Needs info| ask[Ask for missing info]
107|    ask --> start
108|    style done fill:#CDF4D3,stroke:#66D575
109|```
110|
111|### A flow split across two diagrams
112|
113|Divide the ordered source list into groups of at most 9 nodes before the first Mermaid block, each group ending on a hand-off node that names it, so the split is read off the sources rather than a model that already overran. A flow over 9 nodes ends the first diagram on a named hand-off and starts the second diagram from the same name. Both diagrams go into the same file as two boards, read left to right: the second write passes the `fileKey` the first one used, and each board's `%% title:` carries its ordinal and its hand-off, such as `1. Sign up` and `2. Setup`. Every source step lands in one of the diagrams or is listed as left out under the provenance table.
114|
115|```mermaid
116|flowchart TD
117|    start([Sign up]) --> verify[Verify the email]
118|    verify --> profile[Fill in the profile]
119|    profile --> handoff([Continue to setup])
120|    style handoff fill:#CDF4D3,stroke:#66D575
121|```
122|
123|```mermaid
124|flowchart TD
125|    handoff([Continue to setup]) --> connect[Connect an account]
126|    connect --> done([Dashboard shown])
127|    style done fill:#CDF4D3,stroke:#66D575
128|```
129|
130|---
131|
132|## 3. PROVENANCE TABLE
133|
134|One row per item, written in the intake before any Mermaid, beside the model and never on the board. An item is a node, a state, a participant, an entity, a task or an edge. An edge earns a row whenever it was inferred rather than read off a source, because a row kept only for an edge whose ends differ leaves an inferred connector unclassified.
135|
136|| Item | Kind | Source | Source class | Confidence | Rung |
137||---|---|---|---|---|---|
138|| start | node | `<screenshot file, Figma node or doc section>` | current behavior | high | stated |
139|| valid | node | `<source that states the check>` | current behavior | high | stated |
140|| start to valid | edge | `<neighbouring frames with no stated move>` | current behavior | medium | `<ladder step>` |
141|
142|The source class is one of current behavior, approved direction, proposal, retired material and unknown. A row marked proposal or unknown carries its status into the node label, or the node is left out.
143|
144|The confidence is `high`, `medium` or `low`. `high` is an item a source states, `medium` is an item one source implies and `low` is an item the ladder reached by joining two sources. Confidence is not the Brief's status, which says whether a row was captured, so the two sit on one item without repeating each other. The rung is the step of the inference ladder in `references/flow-mode.md` Section 4 that produced the row, and it reads `stated` when a source states the item outright.
145|
146|A `medium` or `low` row carries its uncertainty in the node label or is left out, so the board never shows a confident shape over a thin source. A board has no marker to hide, so the label is where the uncertainty lives.
147|
148|Where a frame name and the frame's visible heading differ, both are recorded in the row and the heading labels the node, because the heading is what the reader sees. The difference is a finding for the playback and is never resolved in the row.
149|
150|Below the table, list every source item that is in no diagram, each with its reason. This is the fidelity ledger sk-design-diagram asks for, so a split or a cut at a lower detail level is named here too:
151|
152|```text
153|Left out: <source item>, <reason, such as retired material, a split that ends before it or a cut at the simplified detail level>
154|```
155|
156|---
157|
158|## 4. REPLY SHAPE
159|
160|```text
161|<board URL>
162|Read-back: <counts the type's reference names, each as n of n>
163|Extensions: <n> of <n> pins, <n> of <n> legend stickies, <n> overlaps
164|Left out: <source item>, <reason>
165|Finding: <a read-back finding, a write warning, an open item or a question>
166|HVR self-scan: <n> hard blockers. Fixed: <terms>. Kept with reason: <terms>.
167|```
168|
169|The `Read-back:` counts follow the type: nodes, connectors and labelled decision exits for a user flow, lanes as well for a process, participants and messages for a sequence, states and transitions for a state diagram, entities, relationships and attributes for an ER diagram, and sections, tasks and milestones for a gantt chart. The `Extensions:` line appears only when the write added any, and the `Left out:` line only when the provenance table lists items left out, so the user sees what the board does not hold. When only a screenshot could be read, the read-back line ends with `, read visually`, because a picture cannot prove which nodes a connector joins. When the connector has no read tool, the line is `Read-back: not possible, the connector has no read tool`, and the board is never called done.
170|
171|These lines are the whole reply, and the self-scan is always the last. Each finding, warning, open item or question is one `Finding:` line, and nothing follows the self-scan. The playback of the settled rows runs before the model and the gate, as `references/flow-mode.md` Section 8 sets out, and it never becomes a line here.
172|
173|---
174|
175|## 5. INTAKE QUESTIONS
176|
177|The type table in `references/flow-mode.md` Section 3 reads as questions. Ask them as an interview before the model is written, in three rounds that depend on each other, because an answer in one round settles what the next round may ask.
178|
179|| Round | Asks | Settles |
180||---|---|---|
181|| One | The reader, the question and the outcome | Who the board is for, what it must answer and what the reader decides next |
182|| Two | Entry, exit and actors | Where the flow starts, where it ends and who takes each step |
183|| Three | Decisions, states, sources and class | Where the flow branches, which states exist, which source states each fact and what class that source holds |
184|
185|### Every question carries a reading and a recommendation
186|
187|A user who does not know an answer should still be able to accept one, so every question is put in this shape:
188|
189|```text
190|Reading: <what the sources already show for this question>
191|Question: <the one thing still open>
192|Recommended: <the answer the AI would take>
193|Why: <the one line of reason>
194|```
195|
196|- One to three questions per round and no later round while an earlier one is open
197|- Never a question a supplied source already answers, because that answer is stated as the reading instead
198|- A round closes when each of its questions is answered, accepted or corrected
199|
200|### A vague answer is asked again
201|
202|An answer that names nothing is asked once more with one probe from this set, and never with the same wording twice:
203|
204|- A concrete scenario, such as one example walked from the first click to the end
205|- An edge case, such as two of these arriving at once
206|- A contradiction, such as one source stating this and another stating the opposite
207|- A term, such as what one word means in this product
208|- A scale, such as how many of these exist on a busy day
209|- A failure mode, such as what the reader sees when one step fails
210|- A boundary, such as where this flow stops and another one begins
211|
212|### An unanswered question is never a dead end
213|
214|When the user skips a question or says they do not know, the AI takes the recommended answer. That fact is marked assumed in the Brief and named in the playback before the gate, so the user corrects it before anything is written. A row the user corrects is recorded as `corrected` and counts as settled. No later round asks it again.

 15|# FigJam Diagram Quality Rubric
 16|
 17|The script checks what a script can see. This rubric is the rest: whether the diagram should exist, whether every node earns its place and whether the reader can trust what lands on the board. Walk it after the check passes and before the write gate.
 18|
 19|**Loading Condition:** CONDITIONAL, on every Flow route before the write gate
 20|**Purpose:** The judgement pass between the pre-write check and the gate
 21|**Scope:** The model, the provenance table, the planned extensions and, after the write, the board and the reply
 22|
 23|---
 24|
 25|## 1. TYPE FIT
 26|
 27|- [ ] The type answers the reader's question, as `references/flow-mode.md` Section 3 maps it
 28|- [ ] A table, a list or a paragraph would not do the same job. If it would, say so and offer that instead
 29|- [ ] The type's reference in `references/types/` was loaded and its judged-by-hand rules were applied
 30|- [ ] A request for a kind Flow Mode does not draw was answered with the nearest type it does draw, or a plain no
 31|
 32|---
 33|
 34|## 2. THE REMOVE TEST
 35|
 36|sk-design-diagram's highest-quality move is usually deletion. A diagram is done when nothing can be removed.
 37|
 38|The remove test runs on the outline before the first Mermaid block, because a step cut from a list of steps costs a sentence and the same step cut from a drawn diagram costs a redraw. This section is the third rung of the challenge ladder in `references/flow-mode.md` Section 3, so the two rungs above it are asked first: what the board must not do, and whether a list, a table or a paragraph would serve the reader better.
 39|
 40|- [ ] The `userIntent` sentence was agreed in the sparring and is the first line of the outline, rather than composed at the write call
 41|- [ ] The remove test ran on the outline, one line per node and edge, before any layout was judged
 42|- [ ] An unanswered sparring proposal is marked assumed and named in the playback before the gate
 43|- [ ] No node can be removed without the reader losing a step they need
 44|- [ ] Every node serves the `userIntent` sentence, or it is cut and named under `Left out:`
 45|- [ ] No two nodes always travel together. If they do, they are one node
 46|- [ ] No connector restates what the layout already shows
 47|- [ ] No label repeats what the shape already says
 48|- [ ] No diagram carries the same label on four or more connectors. Cut them all, or keep one where the label says something the shape cannot. Decision exits and sequence messages are exempt, and an architecture renames each edge instead, as its type reference sets out
 49|- [ ] The remove test ran on the outline before the first Mermaid block, so no node was drawn only to be cut
 50|- [ ] The diagram sits inside its budget, or was split, and every cut is named under `Left out:`
 51|
 52|---
 53|
 54|## 3. SIGNAL
 55|
 56|The marked node is chosen against a target written down first. A board judged only against itself cannot catch a second focal object, such as a title that repeats the claim the marked node was meant to carry. Three lines are written before the first Mermaid block:
 57|
 58|1. **First glance.** The one claim, decision or object that should win within two seconds
 59|2. **Second glance.** The evidence or relationship that advances it
 60|3. **Last glance.** The risk, the metadata or the appendix that stays available without competing
 61|
 62|Those three lines travel into the gate, so the marked node is chosen from them and the reply can say what should win. After the first glance, filled shapes and their keyed fills outweigh connector labels and text in the overview, so the lines name a filled group such as the gray end states before the labels between them.
 63|
 64|- [ ] One accent on a user flow or a process, on the node a reader would keep if they could keep only one, never the node that comes first. The goal, a failure end, a decision and the one step in focus are the candidates, as `references/style-guide.md` Section 3 sets out. Two that tie mean the diagram splits
 65|- [ ] The three glance lines were written before the model and named in the gate
 66|- [ ] On a user flow or a process the first glance is the accented node, marked by the one `style` line the check requires, and the gate names it. On any other type it is the node, message or task a `%% focus:` line names, or, when the model has none, whatever the layout shows first, and the gate says which. The first glance is one node, message or task, never a group such as the end states, and when the layout would show another first, a `%% focus:` line marks it, so the gate never promises a first glance the board does not show. It is the claim the reader came for rather than the node the flow reaches first, and nothing the second or last glance owns competes with it
 67|- [ ] No title repeats the focal claim, so one idea carries one focal object. Where the title already states the claim, the marked node carries the evidence, the consequence or the next move
 68|- [ ] The title names what the reader is looking at, the subtitle says in one sentence who reads it and why, and the source line names the sources and what was left out
 69|- [ ] Shape and label carry the meaning on their own, so the diagram reads in greyscale
 70|- [ ] The key the composer draws names every kind, line and arrow the board shows and nothing else, and no note adds a second key beside it
 71|- [ ] Every zone carries a name a reader can see, and zones group what belongs together rather than marking a position
 72|- [ ] Every label uses the product's or the source's own words. Proper nouns are never renamed
 73|- [ ] The naming fits the audience: exact component names for engineers, plain verbs for a mixed team, capabilities and outcomes for leadership
 74|- [ ] Nothing was invented to fill a lane, a slot or a gap. A missing step is asked about or named, never guessed
 75|
 76|---
 77|
 78|## 4. PROVENANCE
 79|
 80|- [ ] Every node has a row in the provenance table naming its source and its source class
 81|- [ ] Nothing marked proposal or unknown is drawn as current behavior. Its status sits in its label, or it is left out
 82|- [ ] Every causal edge is stated by its sources from both ends. An edge one source states and another contradicts is a finding, not a connector
 83|- [ ] A contradicted item leaves a trace the reader can see. It sits in the reply's `Left out:` line with both sources and the reason, or the one question that asks which source governs settled it. Nothing is removed in silence and no extra line is invented for it
 84|
 85|---
 86|
 87|## 5. THE CHECK AND THE GATE
 88|
 89|- [ ] `scripts/flow_check.py` printed `PASSED` for the model file, with the type each diagram was read as
 90|- [ ] The measures printed beside the counts were read: the widest rank, the longest path, the connectors per step, the average label length and the crossing pairs, against the budgets `scripts/figjam_checks/layout.py` sets
 91|- [ ] A measure out of band was fixed in the model rather than on the board and the check rerun after the change, because the composer owns the layout and a tangled shape is never rearranged after the write
 92|- [ ] `scripts/compose_board.py` printed `COMPOSED` for every diagram, with the counts the read-back will look for
 93|- [ ] The gate message names the plan, the file, what will be written, any planned extensions, the calls the write will spend and the rollback
 94|- [ ] On the generated fallback, an architecture call carries `useArchitectureLayoutCode`, and no other type carries it
 95|
 96|---
 97|
 98|## 6. THE BOARD
 99|
100|After the write, before the reply:
101|
102|- [ ] The read-back counts match the model, as the type's reference sets them out
103|- [ ] Each provenance row whose class is not current behavior or whose edge is inferred was re-read against its source before the gate, and the row records the reason. A row that quotes a source line was not re-read
104|- [ ] The write returned no warning, and its counts match the counts the model expects
105|- [ ] The `COMPOSED` line named the design the board was drawn in, and each `DESIGN` warning it counted became a `Finding:` line naming the token and the shipped value the board used instead
106|- [ ] The overview is the screenshot the composing call returned, and `get_figjam` supplies the outline with a screenshot of each node
107|- [ ] A node that needs its own view is read with `get_screenshot` and a node id from that read, because the tool fails without one
108|- [ ] Two screenshots of the board were taken for this pass: one of the whole board in a single frame and one at 100% zoom. Composition is judged on the overview, because a crossing and a crowded label are invisible at reading size
109|- [ ] The overview reads in the order the model plans, and that order was written down before the first screenshot
110|- [ ] The overview shows no connector crossing another, no connector or label on a zone title, no two edges sharing a trunk the model draws apart and no two labels touching
111|- [ ] No edge runs through a zone it neither starts nor ends in. Edges that only arrive may share one magnet and then lie together for no more than 200 pixels
112|- [ ] One screenshot of the diagram shows no stretched shape, no label cut off and no overlap with existing board content
113|- [ ] Every gap a note or a person placed falls in one of the three bands `references/style-guide.md` Section 7 states, and two unrelated groups sit no closer than the text blocks inside a card
114|- [ ] Each zone holds its own nodes and no other, and no zone overlaps another
115|- [ ] The same screenshot shows no connector crossing and no edge that reads as joining the wrong node. Each edge is followed by eye from end to end, because a connector count does not prove that a route is clear
116|- [ ] Every colour on the board matches its entry in the key, the marked node sits where Section 3 places it, and the board answers the `userIntent` sentence without the model beside it
117|- [ ] Every fill on the board resolves to a role in the active design, as `assets/figjam-design.md` holds it, no zone tint shares a hue with a kind inside it or with the accent, and no note added a colour the design does not name
118|- [ ] The marked node reads first, and no other node competes with it
119|- [ ] A screenshot finding is reported, and it is fixed only by reshaping the model and composing again after a yes, inside the two-attempt bound `references/flow-mode.md` Section 9 sets
120|- [ ] Each extension landed where planned and covers no composed node's label
121|- [ ] Nothing was moved, resized or restyled after the write
122|- [ ] Every finding below full marks names the label it sits on, where it sits in the frame, and one fix, which is a model change composed again after a yes or a named composer limit the writer cannot move
123|
124|---
125|
126|## 7. THE DESIGN RUBRIC
127|
128|The checklists above decide whether a board may ship. The design rubric scores how well it reads, so two boards of the same model, or a board before and after a change, can be compared on something firmer than a glance. Score the overview screenshot on nine criteria, each 0, 1 or 2, for a total out of 18. A criterion scores 2 when it holds everywhere on the board, 1 when it holds with one named exception and 0 when it fails in two places or more.
129|
130|| Criterion | Scores 2 when |
131||---|---|
132|| Frame and entry | The board is one framed area with a title, a one-sentence subtitle and one obvious place to start reading |
133|| Reading order | The flow runs in one direction, the main route sits on one straight line and every branch sits beside it rather than across it |
134|| Colour by meaning | Every colour names a kind the key explains, and nothing is coloured for looks or by position |
135|| Grouping | Zones, lanes or composite states group what belongs together, each carries a visible name and neighbouring tints differ |
136|| Legibility | At overview zoom every label reads, no text is cut off or crowded and shapes of one kind share one size |
137|| Connector clarity | No connector crosses another or runs through a node or a zone title, two edges never lie on one stretch long enough to carry a label, every label sits on its own edge and clear of every other line and every end joins its node cleanly |
138|| Key and source | The key names every mark and nothing else, and the source line names the sources and what was left out |
139|| Proportion | The board reads wider than tall or close to square, with no tall strip, no large empty region and margins on the grid |
140|| Matches the active design | Every kind draws the pair its role names in `assets/figjam-design.md`, the title block and type sizes match every other board, the key lists its entries in the design's order with the focus last, every line takes the design's look and no zone tint shares a hue with a kind inside it |
141|
142|Every score below 2 names the label or the zone it sits on and one fix, in the same shape Section 6 asks of a finding. A comparison between two boards scores both on the same nine criteria and reports both totals, criterion by criterion, so a gain on one criterion never hides a loss on another.
143|
144|---
145|
146|## 8. THE REPLY
147|
148|- [ ] The board URL first, then the `Read-back:` line, then any `Extensions:` and `Left out:` lines, then any `Finding:` lines, then the `HVR self-scan:` line, with no text after it
149|- [ ] No sentence or key entry ties a colour or a zone tint to a team
150|- [ ] A mismatch is reported as measured, and the board is never called done on one
151|- [ ] No file was written to `export/`, and no Mermaid, HTML, SVG or PNG file was left behind
</file-view>
